title: the-loop CLI configuration
description: Schema for the-loop's CLI config (cli-config.yaml: webhooks/polling/eventLog/collaborators/notifications), read by `the-loop gh-webhook`/`poll`/`sessions`/`events`. Independent of .the-loop/harness-config.schema.json (the per-repo HARNESS/plugin config): the CLI is expected to work across multiple repos, so its config resolves in priority order: --config/-c flag, $THE_LOOP_CLI_CONFIG env var, ./.the-loop/cli-config.yaml (repo-relative — an operator may choose to track it in a specific repo), else ~/.the-loop/cli-config.yaml. See decision-032. The operator's own notification recipients are DECLARED here (collaborators, same structure as collaborators.schema.json), never looked up from any repo's collaborators.yaml (issue-82, decision-035).

state.description: Where everything the-loop's CLI GENERATES lives (issue-106). One root to back up, relocate or wipe, instead of four independent path defaults. It supplies DEFAULTS only: an explicitly configured path (routing.registryDir, polling.stateFile, eventLog.path, webhooks.ghWebhook.pidfile) is still used verbatim, so an existing config behaves identically.

root.description: Root directory for generated state. Defaults derived from it: portable work-item records `<root>/portable/` (control + poll state — the half that travels between machines), session records `<root>/local/`, event log `<root>/logs/events.jsonl`, receiver pidfile `<root>/gh-webhook.pid`. Issue-128 organised the tree by portability rather than by writer, retiring `polling.stateFile` (the ledger is a directory now) and moving the session registry's default from `<root>/sessions` to `<root>/local`. The pre-issue-128 locations are still READ once per work item, so an upgrade never re-baselines a watched thread or forgets what an authorized user armed.

webhooks.description: Config for the the-loop CLI webhook receiver(s), started by `the-loop start` when `ghWebhook.enabled` is true (issue-228).

enabled.description: Whether `the-loop start` brings the GitHub webhook receiver up (issue-228, decision-084). Explicit opt-in: a receiver needs a reachable bind, a secret and GitHub-side configuration, so a config that merely DESCRIBES one must not open a port. The foreground entry point (`python -m the_loop.daemon_entry gh-webhook`, for systemd) runs regardless of it.

secretEnv.description: Env var holding the GitHub webhook secret for HMAC verification (never stored in config).

events.description: GitHub event names of interest. Omitted or empty = the-loop's default set (shown above): every event it can map to a work item, so nothing routable is missed. Setting an explicit list narrows it — keep `issues` and `pull_request` in it, or a closed issue / merged PR never reaches the receiver and its session (plus its tmux session) is never closed; the receiver warns at startup if they are missing (issue-94).

polling.description: Config for the the-loop CLI poller (started by `the-loop start` when `polling.enabled` is true, or directly via `python -m the_loop.daemon_entry poller`) — a pull-based, provider-agnostic alternative to the webhook receiver for hosts a webhook cannot reach. Each entry in `sources` selects a provider (e.g. github) the system interfaces with; the core carries no provider-specific knobs. Dispatch behaviour (harness, runner, spawn policy, templates, registry) is the shared top-level `routing` block — the same one the webhook receiver runs on (issue-142).

enabled.description: Whether `the-loop start` brings the poller up (issue-228, decision-084). Explicit opt-in, never inferred from a non-empty `sources` list — `sources` describes HOW to poll, not that polling is wanted on this host. `the-loop start` names this key when it skips a disabled poller, and `python -m the_loop.daemon_entry poller [--once]` runs one regardless (the cron/systemd form).

intervalSeconds.description: Seconds between poll cycles (applies to all sources).

maxRetries.description: Per-event delivery attempts before the poller gives up (issue-80). A spawn or comment forward whose dispatch keeps failing is retried each cycle up to this many attempts; after that the poller logs a terminal failure (poll.spawn_failed / poll.comment_failed) and ignores the event on later polls until new activity re-arms it. An in-flight (still-processing) dispatch is not counted as a failed attempt.

sources.description: Ordered list of provider-specific poll sources. Each entry MUST name a `provider`; the remaining keys are that provider's own config (unknown to the core).

provider.description: Which poll provider handles this source. Only `github` ships today (jira is reserved for a follow-up).

label.description: Label gating what this source polls. Empty = reuse routing.autoExecuteLabel.

repos.description: [github] Repositories to poll as OWNER/REPO. REQUIRED: no fallback to any repo's harness (plugin) config (.the-loop/harness-config.yaml) — which repos to watch is a CLI-config-only concern (issue-63 review). A source with no repos discovers nothing (list_work_items raises).

routing.description: What happens to an event ONCE ACCEPTED: match it to a work item, route it to that item's registered harness session, or spawn one. Top-level since issue-142, because it is NOT the webhook receiver's — the poller reads every value here verbatim for dispatch and `the-loop sessions` reads it again, so one declaration governs both ingresses and the operator's own control surface (docs/specs/issue-15/design.md, decision-016).

enabled.description: Whether the receiver dispatches events at all (routing off = verify and log only).

registryDir.description: Directory holding one JSON file per registered session — the machine-LOCAL half of a work item's state (a harness conversation id, its cwd, its tmux target). Never track it in git: a copied session record is still counted live, so the duplicate guard would refuse the spawn the other machine needs (issue-128, decision-046). Unset resolves to `<state.root>/local`.

defaultHarness.description: Harness used when spawning a session for an unmatched event.

spawnOnUnmatched.description: Policy for events matching no registered session: 'never' log-and-drop; 'always' spawn+register a new session; 'labeled' spawn only when the issue/PR carries autoExecuteLabel.

autoExecuteLabel.description: Issue/PR label that opts a work item into autonomous execution (spawnOnUnmatched: labeled). Read from the webhook payload, no API call.

control.description: Execution control: the keywords an AUTHORIZED user steers the-loop with, in a comment on the work item or its PR (issue-106). Before this, `authorizedUsers` said WHO may be an input and `autoExecuteLabel` said WHICH items may run — nothing said WHEN, so labelling an issue was itself an irreversible trigger. A comment carrying a declared keyword is interpreted by the-loop and NOT forwarded to the harness; the five session commands are also available as `the-loop sessions start|pause|resume|stop|cleanup`, which post the same keyword back to the ticket (marked as the-loop's own so it is never read back). Control parsing runs strictly AFTER the existing guards — the self-comment marker and authorizedUsers — so it never becomes a second, weaker way in; the parser recognises the fixed vocabulary only and yields one of the declared commands, never text from the comment.

enabled.description: Recognise control keywords in comments. false forwards every comment to the harness as before issue-106 (and, with requireStartCommand, disables the start requirement with it).

requireStartCommand.description: BEHAVIOUR CHANGE (issue-106): the auto-execute label becomes NECESSARY BUT NOT SUFFICIENT. With the default true, a labelled work item is *armed*, and a session spawns only once an authorized user has issued the start command for it (by comment, or `the-loop sessions start`) — the request is durable, so it survives a daemon restart, and a later stop/pause disarms it again. This applies to `spawnOnUnmatched: always` too: 'always' widens which items may spawn, never who may start them. Set false to restore the pre-issue-106 behaviour where the label alone starts a session.

keywords.description: The declared vocabulary. Matched as whole tokens, case-insensitively, anywhere in a comment body. Setting one to an empty string disables that command; a comment carrying two DIFFERENT commands is refused outright (nothing executed, nothing forwarded).

execute.description: Answers the graph's `phase-selection` gate (issue-177): the authorized user has chosen which phases this work item needs, so freeze that selection and start walking. Unlike the session commands it does NOT touch the session registry — it neither arms nor disarms — and the comment carrying it is still delivered, because the gate itself is what reads the selection.

contribute.description: Arms the work item exactly as `start` does — same spawn policy, same durable record, same named-actor authorization — and additionally selects the CONTRIBUTION loop (`pdlc-contribution-loop`, issue-185) for its outer walk: the-loop joins an EXISTING, in-progress issue or PR as a contributor rather than owning it from scratch. That loop refuses to begin until an authorized user has stated a goal and success criteria (a `Goal:` line plus a `Success criteria:` bullet list, in one comment — the comment carrying this keyword qualifies), and its phases are sized for a scoped intervention.

do.description: Arms the work item exactly as `start` does — same spawn policy, same durable record, same named-actor authorization — and additionally selects the AD-HOC loop (`pdlc-adhoc-loop`, issue-225) for its outer walk: a tactical task that runs NO PDLC process. That loop has three nodes (`work` -> `review`, back to `work` while the requester asks for more, then `complete`), no spec chain, no phase-selection gate, no artifact gates and no review chain; the-loop does the work, reports back, and treats any authorized reply that is not a declaration of completion as more work. Typing this keyword IS the declaration that the item runs without the process — it is recorded in the portable control record and then in `graph-state.json`, so a reviewer of the resulting change can see that no review chain ran and who decided that. Set to an empty string to disable the word entirely.

cleanup.description: The other end of the life cycle (issue-186): release the LOCAL resources this work item accumulated — the tmux session of every endpoint (its own plus one per pull request), the workspace checkout, and the machine-local session record. DESTRUCTIVE and deliberately unconditional: it ignores `tmux.keepSessionOnClose` and `workspace.keepCheckoutOnClose`, so uncommitted work in the checkout is gone. It keeps the PORTABLE record (control, poll, frozen graph) — that is persistence and tracking, not a resource — and performs NO remote action: no branch, pull request, issue or label is touched. Works retroactively on any work item the-loop tracked, with or without a live session, and durably disarms the item like `stop`. A closure by an AUTHORIZED user cleans up on its own; a closure that names no actor (or an unauthorized one) defers to this keyword, which is why it exists.

interaction.description: Where a session the daemon drives takes its answers FROM (issue-134). Until this existed, a spawned session was never told whether a human was at its terminal, so the model guessed — and both guesses fail: a session asking interactively when nobody ever attaches to its tmux pane asks into a void, while an operator sitting in an attached tmux pane gets round-tripped through GitHub for no reason. The resolved mode is rendered into every event and spawn prompt through the `$interaction_directive` placeholder; a custom promptTemplate that omits the placeholder gets the directive APPENDED, so the rule cannot be stripped by a template edit. Independent of the mode, iteration on a generated artifact (brainstorm.md, requirements.md/bugfix.md, design.md, tasks.md) always happens in pull-request review — an invariant of the loop, not a setting (decision-052).

mode.description: `work-item`: every question the agent needs answered is posted as a comment on the work item (or its PR) and the session waits for the reply to arrive as a new event. `cli`: a human is attached to the session's terminal, so questions are asked there — the decision's OUTCOME still lands on the work item, because the paper trail is not waived by asking in a terminal. Default `work-item` because it fails safe: a tmux session is attachable, not attended (the-loop announces the attach command precisely because nobody is there yet), so the default must be the channel that reaches a human who was not watching. An unrecognised value resolves to `work-item` with a warning, never to `cli`. That one is a warning rather than a refusal — the operator may be piping the harness somewhere the-loop cannot see.

graph.description: Whether dispatch also drives the-loop's process graph (issue-113). Before this, the ingress and the graph never met: spawning a session left the work item's graph unentered (so the `loop:<phase>` labels were never written by the entry hooks), and an arriving comment never reached the human gate waiting for it. With this enabled, a spawn enters the graph's start node and a delivered event advances at most one node boundary, carrying the event's comments to the gate's `classify-feedback`. It is best-effort: a graph failure is logged (`graph.link_failed`) and never costs the delivery. The same block serves the poller, which reuses this routing config.

enabled.description: Couple dispatch to the process graph. False restores the pre-issue-113 behaviour (the graph only moves when a human or CI runs `the-loop graph advance`).

repoHooks.description: Whether this machine runs the WATCHED REPOSITORIES' own graph hooks (issue-248). A repository declares them under `graph.hooks` in its harness config, and that declaration is the opt-in — a repository that declares none is unaffected either way. Left true, the-loop imports the modules a repository names and runs them at the boundaries it named; the code executes inside the-loop's process, with its environment, so adopting a repository's hooks is adopting its code. Set false to refuse the mechanism machine-wide: nothing from any repository is imported, and a repository that declared hooks is named in a warning rather than silently losing its gates. `the-loop graph hooks --repo <path>` reports what a repository declares without importing any of it.

specDir.description: OPTIONAL OVERRIDE. Where specs live in the session's checkout. Leave unset (the default): each work item's own repository declares this as `workflow.specDir` in its harness config, defaulting to `docs/specs` — which is the only thing that works for a daemon watching several repositories with different layouts (decision-032, decision-044). Setting it here overrides every watched repository, and exists for a checkout that carries no harness config at all. A work item with no directory under the resolved path is skipped (recorded as `graph.skipped`), which is what makes the coupling inert for repos that keep no specs. issue-123.

authorizedUsers.description: SECURITY (prompt-injection guard): GitHub logins whose actions the-loop may act on. Comments/reviews/labels/items authored by anyone not listed are ignored by BOTH the webhook receiver and the poller. REQUIRED to actually route anything: no fallback to any repo's harness (plugin) config (.the-loop/harness-config.yaml) — which logins may trigger the daemon is a CLI-config-only concern (issue-63 review). Empty means human-authored events are all ignored (fail closed). Each operator runs their own instance for their own logins.

spawnWorkdir.description: Working directory for sessions spawned on unmatched events. Used only when routing.workspace.root is unset; when a workspace root is configured, spawned sessions run in a per-work-item git worktree instead (issue-76, decision-034).

workspace.description: Per-work-item checkout workspace for spawned sessions (issue-76, decision-034). When `root` is set, the dispatcher checks out each event's repo under the workspace root (layout depends on `strategy`) and runs the spawned session there, instead of the static spawnWorkdir. Auth is the operator's own git credentials (e.g. `gh auth setup-git`).

root.description: Absolute path to the workspace root where repos are checked out (e.g. ~/.the-loop/workspace). Empty (the default) disables the workspace: spawned sessions fall back to spawnWorkdir.

strategy.description: Checkout layout. 'worktree': one shared clone per repo at <root>/<host>/<owner>/<repo> plus one git worktree per work item under <root>/.worktrees/… — concurrent work items on a repo share objects (cheap). 'clone': one folder per work item at <root>/.work-items/<slug>/ with a full clone of each repo it touches — self-contained and simpler to reason about/clean up when a work item spans multiple repos, at the cost of a full clone per work item.

cloneProtocol.description: Preferred clone URL scheme. 'https' uses the payload's clone_url (or https://<host>/<owner>/<repo>.git); 'ssh' uses ssh_url (or git@<host>:<owner>/<repo>.git).

defaultHost.description: Host directory used when the event payload carries no html_url to infer it from (e.g. the poller's leaner payloads). Set to your enterprise domain for a GHE deployment.

keepCheckoutOnClose.description: Keep a work item's checkout after its PR is merged/closed (for post-mortem) instead of removing it — the worktree (worktree strategy) or the work-item folder (clone strategy). In worktree strategy the shared per-repo clone is always kept regardless.

gitBinary.description: Path/name of the git binary used for clone/worktree operations.

tmux.description: Lifetime of the tmux-hosted sessions every dispatch runs in — issue-86. Both defaults keep a finished session readable: a human most wants the transcript of what the agent did exactly when the work item completes.

keepSessionOnClose.description: Leave the tmux session running when the work item's session is closed (PR merged/closed, or `the-loop sessions close`), so the transcript stays attachable; the registry entry is closed either way. false restores the pre-issue-86 kill-on-close. Retained sessions accumulate until the host reboots or you kill them — `the-loop sessions list --status closed` shows them, and a new spawn for the same work item reclaims the deterministic `loop-<slug>` name.

remainOnExit.description: Set tmux's `remain-on-exit` on spawned sessions so the pane and its scrollback survive the harness process exiting (best-effort: an older tmux that rejects it only warns). Events delivered to a session whose pane has died still trigger the issue-80 respawn — a dead pane never silently swallows an event.

resumeOnRespawn.description: When a dead tmux session is respawned (issue-80/issue-89), continue the SAME harness conversation — `claude --resume <recorded session id>` — instead of booting a blank one, so the agent keeps everything it knew about the work item. The registry keeps that session id, so repeated crashes converge on one conversation. The respawn is verified (see resumeProbeSeconds) and falls back to a fresh conversation whenever it cannot be: the harness has no interactive resume (anything but Claude Code today), the recorded id is malformed or absent, tmux failed, or the resumed harness exited immediately. false restores the pre-issue-89 behaviour (always a fresh conversation).

killHarnessOnClose.description: When a work item closes (issue closed, PR merged/closed, or `the-loop sessions close`) and its tmux session is KEPT, end the harness process running inside it — so the retained pane is a readable record of what happened and not a live, writable claude/cursor TUI a stray keystroke or paste could resume (issue-94). SIGTERM, escalating to SIGKILL after harnessKillGraceSeconds; `remain-on-exit` is re-set first so the pane and its scrollback survive the process. Best-effort: a missing session or an already-dead pane never blocks the close. false restores the pre-issue-94 behaviour (a retained session keeps its harness running). Irrelevant when keepSessionOnClose is false — killing the tmux session ends the harness with it.

harnessKillGraceSeconds.description: How long killHarnessOnClose gives the harness to exit after SIGTERM before sending SIGKILL. 0 escalates immediately.

resumeProbeSeconds.description: How long a resume-on-respawn waits before checking that the harness is still running. `tmux new-session -d` succeeds as soon as the pane forks, while a harness that cannot resume (e.g. `claude --resume <unknown-id>`) exits within a fraction of a second — without this probe such a respawn would report success forever while events went nowhere. 0 checks immediately without waiting.

sessionPerPr.description: How many tmux+claude sessions a work item's pull requests get (issue-172, issue-258). `never`: every PR's events are delivered into the work item's single session — the pre-issue-172 behaviour. `cross-repository` (the default): only a PR in a repository OTHER than the work item's gets its own tmux session and harness conversation; a PR in the work item's own repository is that work item's own delivery, on its branch and in its checkout, so it routes to the work item's session (issue-253). `always`: every PR delivering the work item gets its own session, its own repository included. In every mode an endpoint spawns only when it has a WORKING TREE of its own (decision-088 D2), so `always` needs `routing.workspace.root` set, and in practice `strategy: clone` — two git worktrees of one clone cannot both hold the PR's branch. A refusal is delivered into the work item's session and recorded as `session.pr_session_declined`. Endpoints are recorded on the work item's single session record and spawned lazily; a PR closing ends only that PR's session. The legacy booleans still parse: `true` is `cross-repository`, `false` is `never`. This value is the **DEFAULT** (issue-260), not the verdict: each work item chooses its own at `phase-selection` (the `pr-sessions-*` checklist rows, this value pre-ticked), an authorized `the-loop execute` freezes it into that work item's portable record, and routing reads it there first. This key answers for every work item that left the rows alone.

webTerminal.description: Optional ttyd-served browser terminal onto the tmux sessions. No auth of its own — access control is environmental: localhost, VPN, or the hosting provider's network (decision-021).

enabled.description: Serve tmux sessions over HTTP via ttyd (verified at receiver start).

host.description: Interface/IP ttyd binds. Keep 127.0.0.1 unless the network layer protects wider exposure.

maxConcurrentDispatches.description: Cap on harness dispatches running in parallel (per-session dispatch is always serialized).

dedupCacheSize.description: Bounded LRU of X-GitHub-Delivery ids for at-most-once processing.

dispatchTimeoutSeconds.description: Timeout for a single dispatch (tmux spawn/paste, including workspace preparation).

promptTemplate.description: string.Template rendered into the prompt that resumes a session. the-loop's internal template; the dispatcher falls back to a built-in default when the path is absent (the case in a project repo, which does not carry the-loop's templates). Set a repo-relative path to override.

spawnPromptTemplate.description: string.Template rendered into the prompt for a newly spawned (auto-execute) session — kicks off the-loop's work-on flow. the-loop's internal template; the dispatcher falls back to a built-in default when the path is absent. Set a repo-relative path to override.

harnessArgs.description: Extra CLI args per harness (e.g. permission flags). The dispatcher never widens permissions itself.

harnessTrust.description: Pre-seed the harness's own config before spawning a session, so it starts working instead of stopping on an interactive dialog (issue-90, decision-036). Claude Code's workspace-trust dialog and bypass-permissions disclaimer are not permission rules, so no CLI flag — `--dangerously-skip-permissions` included — silences them, and every per-work-item checkout is a brand-new directory that trips the trust dialog. Before each spawn/respawn the dispatcher marks that directory trusted in the harness's user config (`projects[<dir>].hasTrustDialogAccepted` + `hasCompletedProjectOnboarding`), honouring `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`. BOTH keys are always written on the EXACT spawn directory (and its realpath), under every `scope`, because the harness reads each of them from the exact project key on at least one path — `scope` only decides whether trust ADDITIONALLY widens to an ancestor (issue-136, decision-052). Writes are narrow and non-destructive: only those keys, merged into what is already there, via a temp file + atomic replace, skipped entirely when the value is already correct, and never applied to a file that does not parse as JSON. A failure logs a warning and emits `workspace.trust_failed` but never fails the dispatch. A harness with no such config surface (cursor-agent) is a silent no-op. NOTE what trust means: a trusted checkout's OWN `.claude/settings.json` may pre-approve tool permissions and add directories to the workspace, so pre-trusting a clone honours grants authored by anyone who can push to that repository. `enabled: false` is the opt-out.

enabled.description: Default true — an unattended daemon cannot answer a trust dialog, so this is what makes auto-execute actually run. Set false to leave your harness config untouched and keep the pre-issue-90 behaviour.

scope.description: Whether trust ADDITIONALLY widens to an ancestor. The spawn directory itself is trusted under both values — that is not the choice here (issue-136, decision-052): `hasTrustDialogAccepted` has two readers in the harness, and only one of them walks up from the cwd. The other reads the exact project key with NO walk, and it decides both whether the dialog appears anyway and whether the repository's own `.claude/settings.json` `permissions.allow` / `additionalDirectories` load at all — so an ancestor entry alone leaves a checkout of any repo shipping those grants sitting on the dialog. `hasCompletedProjectOnboarding` has no ancestor walk either. `workspace-root` (default, owner decision on PR #92) writes a SECOND trust entry on `routing.workspace.root`, so the walking check covers every checkout beneath the root — including folders the-loop never spawned into (a repo you clone there by hand, a nested repo the agent walks into). `directory` keeps trust on the exact spawn directory only — least privilege, one entry per work item; use it when the workspace root holds more than the-loop's own checkouts. Safety rails on `workspace-root`: a root that does not actually contain the spawn directory is dropped, and a root broad enough to be meaningless (`/`, or the home directory itself) degrades to per-directory trust with a warning. With no workspace root configured (legacy `spawnWorkdir`) both scopes behave identically.

acceptBypassPermissions.description: Whether to also record the one-time bypass-permissions disclaimer acceptance (`skipDangerousModePermissionPrompt` in the user settings file, plus the legacy `bypassPermissionsModeAccepted` for older builds) — without it, a session configured for bypass mode is prompted or silently downgraded to `default`. `auto` (default) records it ONLY when this harness's `harnessArgs` already ask for bypass mode (`--dangerously-skip-permissions` or `--permission-mode bypassPermissions`), so the-loop never widens permissions you did not request; `always` records it regardless; `never` never does. NOTE the asymmetry with the trust key: trust is per-directory, but this acceptance is a USER-GLOBAL setting — it removes the bypass-mode confirmation from every Claude Code session on the account, interactive ones included, not just the-loop's spawned sessions. That is the only form the harness offers; `never` plus a narrower `--permission-mode acceptEdits` in `harnessArgs` avoids it entirely.

harnessPlugins.description: Enable the-loop's OWN plugin in the harness before spawning a session, so the session actually has the loop (issue-143, decision-054). Everything a spawned session knows about the loop — the `the-loop` skill, the `/the-loop:*` commands, the SessionStart hook stating the operating rules — ships in the plugin; nothing else in the spawn path installs it, so on a machine where nobody ran `/plugin marketplace add` by hand the session worked its ticket as a plain agent. Before each spawn/respawn the dispatcher ensures the harness's USER SETTINGS file (`<config dir>/settings.json`, honouring `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`) carries `extraKnownMarketplaces["the-loop"]` and `enabledPlugins["the-loop@the-loop"]: true` — exactly what `/plugin marketplace add` + `/plugin install` write. Writes are narrow and non-destructive, sharing `harnessTrust`'s writer: only those two keys, merged into what is already there, temp file + atomic replace, skipped entirely when both already hold a value, and never applied to a file that does not parse as JSON. An EXISTING value is never changed — a marketplace of yours keeps pointing where it points, and an `enabledPlugins` entry already set to `false` stays `false`. A failure logs a warning and emits `workspace.trust_failed` but never fails the dispatch; `cursor-agent` has no plugin-configuration surface and is a silent no-op. Independent of `harnessTrust`: either may be switched off without the other. NOTE the scope: `enabledPlugins` in the user settings file is USER-GLOBAL, so the plugin — skill, commands and its SessionStart hook — also loads in Claude Code sessions you start by hand, not only the ones the-loop spawns. `enabled: false` is the opt-out.

enabled.description: Default true — a spawned session that lacks the plugin is told to run a loop it does not have. Set false to leave your plugin configuration untouched; the session then relies on whatever the operator installed by hand (and on a repo-level `.claude/settings.json`, if the checkout ships one).

marketplaceRepo.description: The `owner/repo` the `the-loop` marketplace is registered from, written as `{"source": {"source": "github", "repo": "<this>"}}`. Point it at your fork to run that fork's plugin — which means running whatever code that repository ships, in every session on this machine. Validated as `owner/repo` (nothing else is written) and only ever read from THIS file, never from an event payload or a cloned repository. Set it to the empty string to enable the plugin without registering any marketplace, for an operator who adds the marketplace some other way.

reactions.description: Dispatch-lifecycle emoji reactions on the triggering GitHub entity (issue-84): when the dispatcher picks an event up it reacts with `started` on the comment that triggered it (or the issue/PR itself for presence/label/review events), then `completed` or `error` from the dispatch outcome. Shared by the webhook receiver AND the poller (like the rest of `routing`). Best-effort via the operator's own `gh` CLI: a reaction failure never affects the dispatch, and a missing `gh`, a non-GitHub provider, or an event with no reactable target is a silent no-op. GitHub's reaction palette is fixed (+1 -1 laugh confused heart hooray rocket eyes) — ✅/⁉️ do not exist, so the defaults map each state to the closest supported emoji.

enabled.description: Default true (owner decision, PR #85 — out-of-box visibility is the feature's point). Reacting is the daemon's one WRITE to GitHub, posted with the operator's own gh credentials and reaction-only (no text); it degrades to a silent no-op when gh is absent. Set false to opt out.

started.description: Reaction added when the event is dequeued for delivery/spawn (👀 by default). Empty string skips this state.

completed.description: Reaction added when the dispatch succeeds (🎉 by default — GitHub has no ✅ reaction). Empty string skips this state.

error.description: Reaction added when the dispatch fails or the worker crashes (😕 by default — GitHub has no ⁉️ reaction). Empty string skips this state.

announce.description: Announce a spawned interactive session on its work item (issue-86): when a tmux-mode session is first spawned for a work item, the-loop posts a comment carrying the tmux session name and the `tmux attach -t loop-<slug>` command, so a human reading the ticket can watch it work without digging through daemon logs. Best-effort via the operator's own `gh` CLI: a failure never affects the dispatch, and a missing `gh`, a non-GitHub work item, or a session with no tmux target yet is a no-op. The body is built only from registry fields (work-item ref, tmux target, harness) — never from event payloads, and it carries no paths, session ids or hostnames. A respawn (issue-80) posts nothing further: it reuses the same loop-<slug> name, so the comment already on the ticket stays correct.

enabled.description: Default true (the point of issue-86 is that the attach command reaches the human; matches the `reactions` precedent). This posts TEXT to GitHub with the operator's own gh credentials — set false to opt out.

standingSessions.description: Standing sessions (issue-277): named, long-lived tmux + harness sessions that belong to NO work item — the ones the-loop keeps for itself (watching the work items in flight, recovering a stuck one, anything higher-order). Declared here, brought up by `the-loop start`, addressed by name on the control plane and — optionally — in a Slack thread of their own. EXECUTABLE-ADJACENT CONFIG: an entry names harness arguments and a working directory, and the session runs with your own credentials. Review an entry like code.

enabled.description: Default off: starting the-loop's daemons never becomes consent to spawn agent sessions nobody asked for. With this false, `the-loop start` starts none of them and says so — while `the-loop stop` still stops any that are running, because a session disabled after it was started must stay stoppable.

sessions.description: One entry per standing session. Names must be unique — a duplicate refuses the whole block rather than picking a winner.

name.description: The session's identity everywhere: `loop-standing-<name>` in tmux, `<name>.json` in the registry, `standing:<name>` as a Slack thread binding. Lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, not starting with a hyphen, at most 40 characters — narrow because the value is interpolated into a tmux target and a file name.

description.description: What this session is for, in one line. Shown by `the-loop standing list`; never sent to the harness.

harness.description: Which harness hosts it. Omitted inherits `routing.defaultHarness`. cursor-agent has no pre-assignable conversation id and so cannot host an interactive session — the same limitation work-item sessions have.

harnessArgs.description: Extra CLI arguments for this session's harness. Omitted (not `[]`) inherits `routing.harnessArgs.<harness>`; `[]` explicitly means none. Widening permissions here widens them for an unattended agent — the-loop never adds a permission flag you did not write.

cwd.description: The directory the session runs in. Omitted inherits `routing.spawnWorkdir`. It must exist: a session is never spawned into a directory that is not there.

prompt.description: The session's brief, inline. APPENDED to the-loop's own directive (you own no work item; do not answer a phase gate or post a control keyword on any ticket), never substituted for it. Mutually exclusive with promptFile.

promptFile.description: The session's brief, read from a file at start time (absolute, or relative to where the-loop runs). Same append rule as `prompt`; declaring both refuses the entry, because there is no precedence between them. An unreadable file fails THAT session and no other.

autoStart.description: Whether `the-loop start` brings this one up. False means it is declared but started only on request (`the-loop standing start <name>`), and its being down never fails `the-loop status`.

slack.description: This session's Slack surface. It reuses the central `channels.slack` bot, tokens, verbosity, read mode and authorized-user list — only the channel can differ.

enabled.description: Announce this session in Slack when it starts and bind the resulting thread to it, so an authorized member's replies in that thread are pasted into its terminal. Requires `channels.slack.enabled`; best-effort — a Slack failure never stops the session starting.

channel.description: The channel id this session is announced in (C…). Empty uses `channels.slack.channel`.

collaborators.description: The OPERATOR'S own notification recipients — the same collaborator structure as .the-loop/collaborators.schema.json ($defs/collaborator), declared here rather than looked up: the CLI daemon never reads any repo's collaborators.yaml (issue-82, decision-035). Typically just the operator themself; roles are used by notifications.events to pick recipients.

notifications.description: Which DAEMON-side events notify which roles from the operator's `collaborators` above (issue-82, decision-035). Disjoint from the harness-side taxonomy in harness-config.yaml (decision pending, PR review, …) — those are raised by the harness inside a repo checkout; these concern the daemon itself.

events.description: Event → roles to notify. Omitting an event means nobody is notified for it.

work-item-spawned.description: A session was spawned for a work item (auto-execute label or spawnOnUnmatched: always).

dispatch-failed.description: A harness dispatch failed terminally (poll.spawn_failed / poll.comment_failed after maxRetries, or a webhook dispatch error).

session-died.description: A registered tmux session was found dead (and respawned when possible — issue-80).

event-dropped-unauthorized.description: An event was dropped by the authorized-actor guard (routing.authorizedUsers).

channels.description: Communication channels (issue-245): named surfaces the-loop holds a back-and-forth conversation on, each with its own event filter and verbosity. Distinct from `integrations` (transports for the-loop's own calls): a channel also reads, and mirrors every reply onto the work item — the single source of truth — with the self-authored marker.

slack.description: The Slack BOT channel — the official slack-sdk WebClient, a bot token, one Slack channel, one thread per work item. THE Slack surface: the graph's notify hook broadcasts through it too (the old integrations.slack incoming webhook was removed — issue-245, PR #267).

enabled.description: Default off: enabling the daemons never becomes consent to posting into (or reading from) a Slack workspace.

botTokenEnv.description: Env var holding the bot token (xoxb-, chat:write plus channels.history for reads). Read at call time; the token value itself is never a config value and never reaches state files or the event log.

appTokenEnv.description: Env var holding the app-level token (xapp-, connections:write) that `the-loop channels listen` needs for Socket Mode — the no-polling read transport.

channel.description: The Slack channel id the bot posts into (C…, from the channel's details pane — ids, not names, survive renames). Empty disables posting.

events.description: Event-type allow-list: only these are posted to this channel. session.awaiting_input is the ask (`the-loop ask`); the graph's notify hook posts its notification events here too (phase-approval-pending, pr-review-pending, decision-pending, security-sign-off-pending, conflict-escalated) — add the ones you want. See `the-loop events --types` for the catalog.

verbosity.description: quiet = one line + the work-item link; normal = + the question text; verbose = + context detail. Strict supersets, so turning it down never changes the words.

authorizedUsers.description: Slack MEMBER IDS (U…, not display names — names are attacker-chosen) whose replies the-loop acts on. Empty denies every reply (fail closed), the routing.authorizedUsers posture.

read.description: How replies come back. Both transports read ONLY threads the-loop itself started.

mode.description: poll = the daemons fetch thread replies on a background thread (and `the-loop channels poll` runs one cycle); socket = `the-loop channels listen` receives them over Socket Mode; off = nothing is read. An unknown value resolves to off, never to a reading mode.

intervalSeconds.description: Poll-mode cadence. A cycle with no bound threads makes no API call at all.

eventLog.description: Structured JSONL event log of every routing/dispatch/session decision made by the-loop's CLI processes (gh-webhook, poll, sessions). Queried with `the-loop events`; schema in skills/the-loop/reference/observability.md (decision-025). Top-level here (not nested under an `observability` key) — the CLI config has no dev/runtime log-level concept, that stays with the HARNESS config's `observability.devLevel`/`runtimeLevel`/`browserLogging`.

path.description: Append-only JSONL file (git-ignored runtime state). Unset resolves under `state.root` (issue-106) — `.the-loop/logs/events.jsonl` with the default root.

integrations.description: How the-loop's OWN calls reach external services (issue-109). This governs the control plane only — what the AGENT does from inside its session is unconstrained (CLI, MCP, API, whatever the harness has). Transport is a choice, not a mandate: `auto` resolves token -> binary and fails closed naming both remedies; an explicit transport is honoured verbatim and fails rather than silently degrading.

transport.description: auto | api (stdlib HTTP + token) | cli (the operator's authenticated gh, inheriting enterprise/SSO)

tokenEnv.description: Env vars holding a token, in order. Never the token itself.

baseUrl.description: API base, e.g. an enterprise host.

service.description: The control-plane API service (issue-161, decision-058/059): the HTTP layer over the-loop's core that the CLI and the MCP endpoint consume. No in-app authentication — a gateway owns that (decision-059); the service's own posture is network scoping: loopback-only unless `exposed` is explicitly true. Hosting the service requires the [service] extra (`pip install 'the-loopy-one[service]'`).

enabled.description: Whether `the-loop start` brings the control-plane service up (issue-228, decision-084). Default true: the service is the CLI's only execution path for core capabilities (decision-058). Setting false also refuses the implicit auto-start (`service.autoStart`) — a service the operator disabled must not resurrect because an unrelated CLI command wanted it.

host.description: Bind host. Non-loopback values refuse to boot unless `exposed` is true — the API can spawn harness sessions with the operator's credentials.

exposed.description: Explicit opt-in to serving beyond loopback. Client authentication stays mandatory either way.

autoStart.description: Whether a CLI command may boot a local service on demand when none is reachable (the service is the CLI's only execution path for core capabilities). Honoured only while `service.enabled` is true — a disabled service never auto-starts (issue-228).

mcp.description: The MCP layer the service exposes (issue-161). One flag: whether the streamable-HTTP MCP endpoint is mounted at all.

enabled.description: Whether the service mounts the MCP endpoint at /mcp (issue-228, decision-084). Default true — /mcp has been unconditionally mounted since issue-161, so the flag exists to NARROW a deployment to REST-only (/mcp answers 404 when false), not as a new opt-in.

stream.description: The server-push stream (issue-239): GET /api/v1/stream, text/event-stream. A READ surface over the same records GET /api/v1/events already serves, held open so the control plane re-renders when the workstation changes instead of on a timer. Governed by `service.cors` like every other route — that parity is why the transport is SSE and not a WebSocket, whose handshake is exempt from CORS (docs/specs/issue-239/design.md).

enabled.description: Whether the service serves /api/v1/stream. Default true; false answers 404 and starts no tailer, narrowing a deployment to REST-only exactly as `service.mcp.enabled` does. An ABSENT block means unconfigured, not disabled.

maxSubscribers.description: Simultaneous open stream connections. Beyond this the service answers 503 and never accepts the connection, so an open dashboard cannot starve the REST surface (requirements R5.1, abuse case 1). A value below 1 clamps up: the bound is not configurable away.

keepAliveSeconds.description: Interval between SSE keep-alive comments on an idle connection, which is what stops an intermediary reaping it. Lower it only if something between the browser and the service reaps idle connections faster than this.

hostIngresses.description: Single-process mode (issue-231): with the service enabled, the enabled ingresses (the poller per `polling.enabled`, the webhook receiver per `webhooks.ghWebhook.enabled`) run as background tasks INSIDE the service process — one pid, one logfile — instead of as separate processes. Each hosted ingress still holds its own pidfile flock (under the service's pid), so `the-loop status`/`stop`, the single-instance guarantees and the daemons API answer unchanged, and a standalone daemon already holding a lock is skipped with a warning rather than fought over. Set false to keep the issue-228 split (fault isolation: a wedged ingress cannot share fate with the API); with `service.enabled: false` the ingresses always run standalone regardless of this flag.

cors.description: Which browser ORIGINS may read this service's responses (issue-211, decision-077). Orthogonal to `host`/`exposed`, which decide who may CONNECT: no value here widens the bind. Ships allowing the one origin the-loop publishes its dashboard to, so the hosted UI works against a local service with no configuration; an empty `allowOrigins` installs no middleware at all and restores same-origin-only behaviour.

allowOrigins.description: Exact origins (scheme + host + port, no path) allowed to read responses. Compared exact-string — no prefix, suffix or regex matching. `[]` disables cross-origin access entirely. `"*"` allows every origin and is refused at start-up when `allowCredentials` is true.

allowMethods.description: HTTP methods a cross-origin caller may use. The default is exactly what the shipped dashboard sends.

allowHeaders.description: Request headers a cross-origin caller may send, beyond the browser's safelist. Add `Authorization` when a gateway in front expects a bearer token from the page.

allowCredentials.description: Whether the browser may send cookies/credentials cross-origin. the-loop's own client sends none; enable only for a gateway deployment that authenticates the page. `true` with `"*"` in `allowOrigins` refuses to boot.

allowPrivateNetwork.description: Answer Chromium's private-network preflight (`Access-Control-Allow-Private-Network`) for an ALREADY-allowed origin — what lets a public HTTPS page reach a loopback service. Never widens the origin allowlist.

selfDiagnosis.description: Self-diagnosis (issue-242): when the-loop's own machinery fails — an error-level event or a terminal give-up in the event log — debug it in an isolated agent one-shot and file the findings as an issue on the-loop's own repository, labeled `the-loop: self-diagnosed`. STRICTLY OPT-IN and off by default: enabling it means this machine may post redacted failure reports publicly, using your own `gh` credentials. Everything posted is built from a field allow-list with free text scrubbed (paths, usernames, hostnames, e-mails, tokens, sensitive env values), and a self-filed issue is never armed: no auto-execute label, no control-keyword comment, and the self-authored marker so the-loop's own ingress drops it. Preview what would leave the machine with `the-loop diagnose --dry-run` before opting in.

enabled.description: The opt-in. Only a literal `true` enables anything; an absent section, `false`, or a malformed section all mean no scan, no watcher thread, no agent, no post (fail closed).

repo.description: owner/repo the issues are filed on. Defaults to the-loop's own repository — the point of the feature is fixing the-loop, not your project. Point it at a fork if you triage there first.

label.description: Label requested on each created issue. GitHub silently drops the request for callers without triage rights on the target repository; the body names the intended label either way, so the marker survives the permission gap. Must never equal `routing.autoExecuteLabel` or any `polling.sources[].label`.

harness.description: Which agent harness runs the isolated diagnosis one-shot (the same adapter set as `routing.defaultHarness`).

model.description: Model passed to the harness's one-shot invocation; empty uses the harness's own default.

timeoutSeconds.description: Wall-clock budget for one diagnosis agent run.

intervalSeconds.description: How often the background watcher (hosted inside the poller and gh-webhook daemons) scans the event log for new failures. A manual `the-loop diagnose` scans regardless.

maxIssuesPerDay.description: Rolling 24h cap on created issues (storm control). Candidates over the cap are DEFERRED to a later scan, never dropped.

maxRetries.description: Failed diagnosis attempts (agent or post) per failure fingerprint before it is abandoned and never retried.
